title: Quantum entanglement
summary: See how two particles can stay linked across any distance, and why that still can't send a message faster than light.
objective: Predict what entangled particles show when measured, and explain why they can't be used to send instant messages.

hook.prompt: A lab makes a pair of entangled particles and sends them light-years apart. You measure one particle's spin and get "up". What do you now know about the other one?

options.text: Measured the same way, it will read "down"
Nothing: it's still a 50/50 guess
options.feedback: That's what you'd expect for two separate particles. Entangled ones are different.

options.text: Nothing until a light signal could reach it
options.feedback: Surprisingly, the distance doesn't matter: the link holds however far apart they are.

hook.explanation: Its partner will read the opposite, even light-years away. So how can two particles stay linked like that, and can we use it?

bricks.title: Linked answers, random alone
bricks.body: Particles have a property called **spin**: measure it along a direction and you always get one of two answers, *up* or *down*. Two particles can be made as an **entangled** pair. Measure both the same way and, for the pairs in this lesson, the answers always come out opposite, however far apart they are. Yet each result on its own is random, like a coin flip.

term.definition: A link between particles that makes their measurement results match up, even when each result on its own is random.

visual.alt: A table of four entangled pairs: Ana's results read up, down, down, up, and Ben's read down, up, up, down, always the opposite of Ana's.
visual.html:
PairAna's particleBen's particle
1↑ up↓ down
2↓ down↑ up
3↓ down↑ up
4↑ up↓ down

bricks.prompt: Ana and Ben measure five more entangled pairs the same way. Ana gets up, up, down, up, down. What does Ben get?

options.text: down, down, up, down, up
up, up, down, up, down
options.feedback: That's matching, not opposite. For these pairs, Ben's result is always the opposite of Ana's.

options.text: No way to tell: each of Ben's results is random
options.feedback: Each result is random on its own, but once Ana's result is known, Ben's partner result is fixed: the opposite.

bricks.hint: For these pairs, how does each of Ben's results relate to Ana's?
bricks.explanation: Each of Ben's results is the opposite of Ana's for the same pair, so up becomes down and down becomes up.

bricks.prompt: Ana measures her half of 1,000 entangled pairs and looks only at her own list. What does it look like?

options.text: About half up and half down, in no predictable order
All up, because her particles were made the same way
options.feedback: Being made the same way links each pair, but each single result is still a coin flip.

options.text: Neatly alternating: up, down, up, down
options.feedback: Opposite answers are between the two particles of a pair, not between one of Ana's results and the next.

bricks.hint: What does the lesson say about each result on its own?
bricks.explanation: On its own, each result is random, so Ana's list looks like 1,000 coin flips. The link only shows when you pair her list with Ben's.

bricks.title: Not just a pair of gloves
bricks.body: So far: linked answers, each random alone. A tempting explanation is gloves. Pack a left and a right glove into two boxes; open one and you know the other, because each glove was fixed all along. Physicist John Bell showed this idea can be tested. In **Bell tests**, the two sides measure in different, randomly chosen directions. The pattern of agreements can't be produced by answers each particle carried from the start, and experiments have confirmed this many times.

term.definition: An experiment that checks whether answers fixed in advance, like gloves in boxes, could explain the link between entangled particles.

visual.alt: Two cards side by side. Gloves: each answer fixed when packed. Entangled pair: no answers carried from the start can explain the results.
visual.html:
Gloves in boxes

Each glove is left or right from the moment it's packed. Opening a box just reveals it.

Entangled pair

Bell tests show no answers carried from the start can produce the results.

bricks.prompt: Which idea about entangled particles have Bell tests ruled out?

options.text: Each particle carried a fixed answer from the start, like a glove in a box
The two results stay linked even when the particles are far apart
options.feedback: Bell tests confirmed the link. What they ruled out is the glove-style explanation for it.

options.text: Each result on its own looks random
options.feedback: That's still true. Bell tests are about what explains the link between the two results.

bricks.hint: Which explanation did Bell turn into something you could test?
bricks.explanation: Bell tests show the pattern of agreements can't come from answers each particle carried from the start, so the glove picture fails.

bricks.title: No instant messages
bricks.body: Measuring one particle seems to tell you about its partner instantly. So could Ana send Ben a message? No. Ana can't choose her result: it's random. So Ben's list, on its own, looks like coin flips whatever Ana does. The opposite pattern only appears when they put the two lists side by side, and sharing a list takes an ordinary call or email, which is no faster than light.

visual.alt: Ben's list alone reads up, up, down, up, down and looks random; beside Ana's list, every one of his results is the opposite of hers.

bricks.prompt: Ana wants to send Ben a "yes" right now by measuring her particles. What does Ben see when he measures his?

options.text: A random-looking mix of up and down, with no sign of her message
A sudden run of "down" results that spells out her "yes"
options.feedback: Ana can't choose her results, so she can't force a pattern onto his either.

options.text: Nothing: his particles stop giving results once Ana measures hers
options.feedback: Ben still gets an up or down every time. They just look random to him.

bricks.hint: Can Ana pick what her own results will be?
bricks.explanation: Ana's results are random, so Ben's list looks like coin flips whatever she does. No message gets through.

bricks.prompt: Ana and Ben each measure 1,000 entangled pairs. At which moment can they first see that their results are linked?

options.text: When they put their two lists side by side
As soon as Ana measures her particles
options.feedback: Ana's list alone looks random. She needs Ben's list to see the opposite pattern.

options.text: As soon as Ben measures his particles
options.feedback: Ben's list alone looks like coin flips too. The link hides until the lists meet.

bricks.hint: What does each list look like on its own?
bricks.explanation: Each list alone is random. Only comparing them pair by pair shows the opposites, and that comparison needs an ordinary message.

challenge.prompt: A startup pitches an "entangled phone": "We measure our particles to spell a text, and your partner particles instantly show it, even across the galaxy." What's the flaw?

options.text: The sender can't choose measurement results, so the receiver only ever sees random-looking ones
Entangled particles stop being linked once they're far apart
options.feedback: Distance isn't the problem: the link holds however far apart the particles are.

options.text: Bell tests showed entanglement isn't real
options.feedback: Bell tests confirmed the link. They ruled out the glove-style explanation for it.

options.text: There's no flaw: the link is instant, so the text arrives instantly
options.feedback: The link is real, but each result is random, so there's nothing for the sender to write with.

challenge.hint: Who decides whether a measurement comes out up or down?
challenge.explanation: Results are random, so the sender can't encode a text, and the receiver's list looks like coin flips until the lists are compared by ordinary means.

takeaways: Entangled particles give linked answers when measured the same way, however far apart they are.
Each result on its own is random; the link only shows when you compare both sides.
Bell tests rule out the idea that each particle carried a fixed answer, like a glove.
Entanglement can't send messages faster than light, because nobody can choose the results.
